mechanism: Irreversibly inhibits COX-1 and COX-2, reducing thromboxane A2-mediated platelet aggregation
standard_dosing: Cardiac: 81-325mg daily; Acute MI: 325mg stat; Pain/fever: 325-650mg q4-6h
renal_adjustment: Avoid if GFR <10 mL/min
hepatic_adjustment: Avoid in severe hepatic failure
monitoring: Signs of GI bleeding; renal function with long-term use
content: Aspirin (Acetylsalicylic Acid) is an antiplatelet and NSAID that irreversibly inhibits COX-1 and COX-2 enzymes, reducing thromboxane A2-mediated platelet aggregation and prostaglandin synthesis. It is a cornerstone drug in acute coronary syndrome management. Indications include acute myocardial infarction (STEMI and NSTEMI) at 325mg stat loading dose, stroke prevention, atrial fibrillation, stable angina, and pain/fever management. Cardiac dosing is 81-325mg daily for secondary prevention. Contraindications include active GI bleeding, aspirin hypersensitivity, children with viral illness due to Reye syndrome risk, severe hepatic failure, and third trimester pregnancy. Major drug interactions include warfarin and heparin (increased bleeding risk), SSRIs (increased GI bleed risk), other NSAIDs (additive GI toxicity), and methotrexate (increased methotrexate toxicity and myelosuppression). Common side effects are GI irritation and bleeding, tinnitus at high doses, and bronchospasm in aspirin-sensitive asthma patients. Monitor for signs of GI bleeding and renal function with long-term use. Avoid if GFR below 10 mL/min. Pregnancy category C in first and second trimesters, D in third trimester. Aspirin should not be withheld in acute MI — the mortality benefit far outweighs bleeding risk.

mechanism: Reversibly binds P2Y12 ADP receptor on platelets, inhibiting platelet aggregation
standard_dosing: Loading: 180mg PO; Maintenance: 90mg BID
renal_adjustment: No adjustment needed
hepatic_adjustment: Avoid in severe hepatic impairment
monitoring: Bleeding signs; dyspnea; platelets
content: Ticagrelor is a P2Y12 inhibitor antiplatelet agent that reversibly binds the P2Y12 ADP receptor on platelets, inhibiting platelet aggregation. Unlike clopidogrel, ticagrelor does not require hepatic activation and provides more consistent antiplatelet effect. It is the preferred P2Y12 inhibitor for acute coronary syndromes including STEMI and NSTEMI per ACC/AHA guidelines. Loading dose is 180mg orally, followed by 90mg twice daily maintenance. Contraindicated in active pathological bleeding, prior intracranial hemorrhage, severe hepatic impairment, and with concomitant strong CYP3A4 inhibitors like ketoconazole or clarithromycin. A critical interaction is that aspirin doses above 100mg daily reduce ticagrelor efficacy — always use low-dose aspirin 81mg with ticagrelor. Other interactions include warfarin (increased bleeding), digoxin (increased levels), and simvastatin above 40mg. The most common unique side effect is dyspnea, which occurs in up to 14% of patients and is usually benign and self-limiting but can cause discontinuation. Other side effects include bleeding, bradycardia with ventricular pauses, and hyperuricemia leading to gout flares. No renal dose adjustment needed. Do not use ticagrelor in patients with prior stroke or TIA (increased intracranial bleeding in PLATO subanalysis). Monitor for bleeding signs and dyspnea.

mechanism: Irreversibly blocks P2Y12 ADP receptor; prodrug requiring CYP2C19 activation
standard_dosing: Loading: 300-600mg PO; Maintenance: 75mg daily
renal_adjustment: No adjustment needed
hepatic_adjustment: Caution in moderate; avoid severe
major_interactions: PPIs especially omeprazole (reduces efficacy via CYP2C19 inhibition)
monitoring: CBC; signs of bleeding; CYP2C19 genetic testing if available
content: Clopidogrel (Plavix) is a P2Y12 inhibitor antiplatelet prodrug that irreversibly blocks the P2Y12 ADP receptor on platelets. As a prodrug, it requires hepatic activation via CYP2C19 enzyme. This is clinically critical because patients who are CYP2C19 poor metabolizers have significantly reduced antiplatelet effect and higher rates of stent thrombosis and cardiovascular events. CYP2C19 genetic testing should be performed when available. Loading dose is 300-600mg orally, with 75mg daily maintenance. Used in ACS (STEMI, NSTEMI), stroke prevention with aspirin (POINT/CHANCE trial for minor stroke/TIA), and peripheral artery disease. A major drug interaction is with proton pump inhibitors, especially omeprazole, which inhibits CYP2C19 and reduces clopidogrel activation — use pantoprazole instead if PPI is needed. Other interactions include warfarin and aspirin (additive bleeding), NSAIDs, and other CYP2C19 inhibitors. Rare but serious side effects include thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) and neutropenia. Common side effects are bleeding, rash, and GI upset. No renal adjustment needed. Clopidogrel is generally second-line to ticagrelor for ACS but preferred in patients with prior stroke/TIA or when ticagrelor is not tolerated.

mechanism: Binds antithrombin III, accelerating inactivation of thrombin (IIa), Xa, IXa, XIa, and XIIa
standard_dosing: ACS: 60 units/kg bolus (max 4000u) then 12 units/kg/hr; DVT/PE: 80 units/kg bolus then 18 units/kg/hr
renal_adjustment: Use with caution; monitor aPTT closely
hepatic_adjustment: Use with caution (reduced clearance)
monitoring: aPTT (target 60-100s); platelets q2-3 days (HIT surveillance); anti-Xa levels
content: Unfractionated Heparin (UFH) is an anticoagulant that binds antithrombin III, accelerating the inactivation of thrombin (factor IIa) and factor Xa along with factors IXa, XIa, and XIIa. It is the preferred parenteral anticoagulant in many acute settings due to its short half-life (60-90 minutes), reversibility with protamine sulfate, and IV titratability. Indications include acute coronary syndromes (STEMI/NSTEMI) with weight-based bolus of 60 units/kg (max 4000 units) then 12 units/kg/hr infusion, DVT and PE treatment with 80 units/kg bolus then 18 units/kg/hr, atrial fibrillation bridging, cardiopulmonary bypass, and DIC management. The most feared complication is heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT), an immune-mediated condition causing paradoxical thrombocytopenia AND thrombosis occurring typically 5-10 days after initiation. HIT requires immediate heparin cessation and alternative anticoagulation with argatroban or bivalirudin. Platelet count must be monitored every 2-3 days for HIT surveillance. Other side effects include bleeding, osteoporosis with long-term use, and hyperkalemia from aldosterone suppression. Monitor aPTT targeting 60-100 seconds (or anti-Xa levels). Major interactions include warfarin, aspirin, NSAIDs, and thrombolytics which all increase bleeding risk. Contraindicated in known HIT, active major bleeding, and severe thrombocytopenia.

mechanism: Binds antithrombin III; primarily inhibits factor Xa with less effect on IIa than UFH
standard_dosing: Treatment: 1mg/kg SC BID or 1.5mg/kg SC daily; Prophylaxis: 40mg SC daily or 30mg SC BID
renal_adjustment: CrCl <30: reduce to 1mg/kg SC daily (treatment); 30mg SC daily (prophylaxis)
hepatic_adjustment: No specific adjustment; caution in severe hepatic disease
monitoring: Anti-Xa levels in renal impairment, obesity, pregnancy; platelets
content: Enoxaparin (Lovenox) is a low molecular weight heparin that binds antithrombin III, primarily inhibiting factor Xa with less effect on thrombin (IIa) compared to unfractionated heparin. This provides more predictable pharmacokinetics allowing weight-based subcutaneous dosing without routine aPTT monitoring. Treatment dosing is 1mg/kg subcutaneous twice daily or 1.5mg/kg daily; prophylactic dosing is 40mg subcutaneous daily or 30mg twice daily. Critical renal adjustment: reduce to 1mg/kg once daily when CrCl is below 30 mL/min; avoid entirely if CrCl below 15. Anti-Xa level monitoring is required in renal impairment, obesity (BMI >40), and pregnancy with target 0.6-1.0 IU/mL for BID dosing. Used for DVT and PE treatment, ACS/NSTEMI, VTE prophylaxis post-surgery, and bridge anticoagulation. Contraindicated in HIT, active major bleeding, and CrCl below 15. Interactions include NSAIDs, aspirin, warfarin, and thrombolytics — all increase bleeding risk. Side effects include bleeding, HIT (less common than UFH), injection site hematoma, hyperkalemia, and transient liver enzyme elevation. Unlike UFH, protamine only partially reverses enoxaparin (approximately 60%). Pregnancy category B — preferred anticoagulant during pregnancy over warfarin.

mechanism: Inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, depleting active vitamin K needed for clotting factors II, VII, IX, X, protein C and S
standard_dosing: Individualized; typical 2-5mg daily; adjust to INR 2-3 (2.5-3.5 for mechanical valves)
renal_adjustment: No specific adjustment; monitor INR closely
hepatic_adjustment: Sensitivity increased; start low and monitor closely
monitoring: INR weekly initially, then monthly when stable; signs of bleeding
content: Warfarin (Coumadin) is a vitamin K antagonist oral anticoagulant that inhibits vitamin K epoxide reductase, depleting active vitamin K necessary for synthesis of clotting factors II, VII, IX, and X, as well as proteins C and S. It is the drug of choice for anticoagulation in patients with mechanical heart valves (DOACs are contraindicated) and an alternative for atrial fibrillation, DVT, and PE. Dosing is individualized with typical starting dose of 2-5mg daily, adjusted to target INR 2-3 for most indications or 2.5-3.5 for mechanical valves. Warfarin has one of the most extensive drug interaction profiles of any medication. Critical interactions include amiodarone (markedly increases INR — reduce warfarin dose by 30-50%), fluconazole and other azole antifungals (increase INR), rifampin (potent CYP inducer that markedly decreases INR), vitamin K-rich foods like leafy greens (decrease INR — counsel patients on consistent dietary intake), aspirin and NSAIDs (additive bleeding risk), and antibiotics which alter gut flora and unpredictably affect vitamin K absorption. Monitoring requires INR checks weekly initially then monthly once stable. Pregnancy category X — warfarin is teratogenic causing warfarin embryopathy (nasal hypoplasia, stippled epiphyses). Rare but serious side effects include skin necrosis (due to protein C depletion occurring before anticoagulant factors deplete, particularly in protein C deficient patients) and purple toe syndrome. Reversal: vitamin K for non-urgent, FFP or 4-factor PCC for urgent bleeding.

drug_class: Direct Oral Anticoagulant (DOAC) / Factor Xa Inhibitor
mechanism: Direct inhibitor of factor Xa, preventing conversion of prothrombin to thrombin
standard_dosing: AF: 5mg BID (2.5mg BID if >=2 of: age >=80, weight <=60kg, Cr >=1.5); DVT/PE: 10mg BID x7 days then 5mg BID
renal_adjustment: Reduce for AF per criteria; avoid if CrCl <15
hepatic_adjustment: Avoid in severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh C)
major_interactions: Strong dual CYP3A4+P-gp inducers like rifampin (decrease levels)
monitoring: Renal function annually; signs of bleeding; CBC
content: Apixaban (Eliquis) is a direct oral anticoagulant (DOAC) that directly and selectively inhibits factor Xa, preventing conversion of prothrombin to thrombin. It is the preferred DOAC for non-valvular atrial fibrillation stroke prevention and DVT/PE treatment due to its favorable bleeding profile compared to warfarin and rivaroxaban (lowest GI bleeding risk among DOACs in the ARISTOTLE trial). Standard dosing for atrial fibrillation is 5mg twice daily, reduced to 2.5mg twice daily if the patient meets at least 2 of 3 criteria: age 80 or older, weight 60kg or less, or serum creatinine 1.5 mg/dL or greater. For DVT/PE treatment: 10mg twice daily for 7 days then 5mg twice daily. Contraindicated in active major bleeding, mechanical heart valves, and moderate-severe mitral stenosis. Avoid if CrCl below 15 mL/min and in Child-Pugh C hepatic impairment. Major interactions include strong dual CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein inhibitors (ketoconazole, ritonavir) which increase apixaban levels, and strong inducers like rifampin which significantly decrease efficacy. Reversal agent is andexanet alfa (Andexxa) for life-threatening bleeding. No routine coagulation monitoring is required — a major advantage over warfarin. Monitor renal function annually for dose adjustment. Side effects include bleeding and anemia. Preferred over warfarin for most non-valvular AF patients due to superior efficacy, safety, and convenience.

drug_class: Direct Oral Anticoagulant (DOAC) / Factor Xa Inhibitor
mechanism: Directly and selectively inhibits factor Xa
standard_dosing: AF: 20mg daily with evening meal; DVT/PE: 15mg BID x21 days then 20mg daily
renal_adjustment: AF: avoid if CrCl <15; DVT: avoid if CrCl <30
hepatic_adjustment: Avoid in Child-Pugh B or C
major_interactions: Combined P-gp and strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (increase exposure)
monitoring: Renal function annually; signs of bleeding; CBC
content: Rivaroxaban (Xarelto) is a direct oral anticoagulant that directly and selectively inhibits factor Xa. It offers once-daily dosing for atrial fibrillation (20mg with evening meal) which improves compliance, and has a unique low-dose indication (2.5mg BID with aspirin) for coronary artery disease and peripheral artery disease secondary prevention (COMPASS trial). For DVT/PE treatment, dosing is 15mg twice daily for 21 days then 20mg once daily. Must be taken with food (evening meal for AF) to ensure adequate absorption. Rivaroxaban has higher GI bleeding rates compared to apixaban but comparable efficacy for stroke prevention. Contraindicated in active major bleeding, mechanical heart valves, moderate-severe mitral stenosis, CrCl below 15 (below 30 for DVT treatment), and Child-Pugh B or C hepatic impairment. Major interactions include combined P-glycoprotein and strong CYP3A4 inhibitors which increase drug exposure, rifampin which markedly decreases efficacy, and azole antifungals. Reversal agent is andexanet alfa for life-threatening bleeding. No routine monitoring required. Monitor renal function annually. Extended low-dose prophylaxis (10mg daily) can be used after initial 6 months of treatment for secondary VTE prevention. Side effects include bleeding (GI bleeding more common than with apixaban), nausea, and transient liver enzyme elevation.

mechanism: Selectively blocks beta-1 adrenergic receptors, reducing heart rate, contractility, and blood pressure
contraindications: Severe bradycardia or heart block (without pacemaker)
standard_dosing: AF rate control: 25-200mg daily; Heart failure: start 12.5-25mg daily, titrate up; Hypertension: 50-200mg daily
renal_adjustment: No adjustment needed
hepatic_adjustment: Reduce dose in severe hepatic impairment
monitoring: Heart rate; blood pressure; signs of decompensation
content: Metoprolol Succinate (Toprol-XL) is a beta-1 selective adrenergic blocker that selectively blocks beta-1 receptors in the heart, reducing heart rate, myocardial contractility, and blood pressure. It is one of the most widely prescribed cardiovascular medications. Key indications include atrial fibrillation rate control (targeting heart rate below 110 bpm at rest), hypertension, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF — one of only three beta-blockers with mortality benefit in HF along with carvedilol and bisoprolol), stable angina, post-MI secondary prevention, and migraine prophylaxis. In heart failure, start at very low doses (12.5-25mg daily) and titrate slowly every 2 weeks to target dose, as initiation during acute decompensation can worsen heart failure. Contraindicated in cardiogenic shock, decompensated heart failure (initiate only when euvolemic), severe bradycardia or heart block without a pacemaker, and severe reactive airway disease (asthma — though beta-1 selectivity is lost at higher doses). Critical interactions include verapamil and diltiazem (additive AV nodal blockade causing severe bradycardia or heart block), digoxin (additive bradycardia), and insulin/sulfonylureas (masks the adrenergic symptoms of hypoglycemia like tremor and tachycardia — patients may not recognize low blood sugar). Do not abruptly discontinue — taper over 1-2 weeks to prevent rebound tachycardia and hypertension.

mechanism: Inhibits angiotensin-converting enzyme, reducing angiotensin II and aldosterone, decreasing BP and afterload
standard_dosing: Hypertension: 10-40mg daily; Heart failure: start 2.5-5mg daily, target 40mg; Post-MI: 5mg day 1, titrate
renal_adjustment: CrCl 10-30: start 5mg; CrCl <10: 2.5mg
hepatic_adjustment: No specific adjustment
monitoring: BP; serum creatinine and potassium at initiation, 1-2 weeks, then periodically
content: Lisinopril is an ACE inhibitor that blocks angiotensin-converting enzyme, preventing conversion of angiotensin I to angiotensin II, thereby reducing vasoconstriction, aldosterone secretion, blood pressure, and cardiac afterload. It is a cornerstone of guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (HFrEF), hypertension, post-MI remodeling prevention, diabetic nephropathy, and CKD with proteinuria. For heart failure, start at 2.5-5mg daily and titrate to target dose of 40mg daily. Contraindicated in pregnancy (category D — teratogenic causing renal dysgenesis, oligohydramnios, skull hypoplasia), history of ACE inhibitor-induced angioedema (switch to ARB with caution or use sacubitril/valsartan), bilateral renal artery stenosis (can precipitate acute renal failure), and hyperkalemia. Critical interactions include potassium-sparing diuretics and potassium supplements (hyperkalemia — monitor potassium closely), NSAIDs which reduce antihypertensive effect and increase AKI risk, ARBs (dual RAAS blockade increases hyperkalemia, hypotension, and renal failure without benefit), and lithium (increased lithium levels and toxicity). The hallmark side effect is dry persistent cough occurring in 10-15% of patients due to bradykinin accumulation — if intolerable, switch to an ARB. Angioedema is rare but life-threatening, more common in African Americans. Monitor creatinine and potassium at initiation, 1-2 weeks after starting, and periodically. A rise in creatinine up to 30% above baseline is acceptable and expected.

mechanism: Inhibits Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in thick ascending loop of Henle, causing natriuresis and diuresis
standard_dosing: Heart failure: 40-80mg IV (or 2.5x home oral dose); Oral: 20-80mg daily; Max: 600mg/day
renal_adjustment: Higher doses needed in renal impairment; may need continuous infusion
hepatic_adjustment: Caution (hypokalemia can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy)
monitoring: Daily weight; I/O; BMP (K+, Na+, Cr, BUN); BP; urine output
content: Furosemide (Lasix) is a loop diuretic that inhibits the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle, producing potent natriuresis and diuresis. It is the cornerstone of decongestion therapy in acute decompensated heart failure and pulmonary edema. For acute heart failure, IV administration is preferred: 40-80mg IV bolus if diuretic-naive, or 2.5 times the home oral dose given IV for patients already on oral furosemide. Target urine output of 3-5 liters in the first 24 hours. Also used for resistant hypertension, hepatic and renal edema, hyperkalemia (drives potassium excretion), and hypercalcemia (after adequate hydration). Electrolyte derangements are the most clinically significant side effects: hypokalemia (potassium wasting — always replace potassium and monitor closely), hyponatremia, and hypomagnesemia. Hypokalemia is particularly dangerous in patients on digoxin as it increases digoxin toxicity and arrhythmia risk. Other side effects include metabolic alkalosis, hyperuricemia precipitating gout, hyperglycemia, ototoxicity with high IV doses or rapid administration, and hypotension. Critical interactions: aminoglycosides (additive ototoxicity and nephrotoxicity), digoxin (hypokalemia-enhanced toxicity), NSAIDs (reduce diuretic efficacy), and lithium (increased levels). Higher doses are required in renal impairment due to reduced tubular secretion. In cirrhosis, use cautiously as hypokalemia and alkalosis can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy — always pair with spironolactone in a 40:100 ratio.

mechanism: Inhibits HMG-CoA reductase, the rate-limiting enzyme in cholesterol synthesis, reducing LDL cholesterol
contraindications: Active liver disease or unexplained persistent LFT elevations
Concomitant strong CYP3A4 inhibitors at high doses
standard_dosing: Moderate intensity: 10-20mg daily; High intensity: 40-80mg daily; ACS: 80mg daily
renal_adjustment: No adjustment needed
hepatic_adjustment: Contraindicated in active liver disease
major_interactions: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin, itraconazole — increased statin levels)
monitoring: Lipid panel at 4-12 weeks; LFTs at baseline; CK if myalgia symptoms
content: Atorvastatin (Lipitor) is an HMG-CoA reductase inhibitor (statin) that blocks the rate-limiting enzyme in hepatic cholesterol synthesis, reducing LDL cholesterol by 30-50% depending on dose. It is one of the most prescribed medications worldwide and a cornerstone of cardiovascular prevention. High-intensity statin therapy (atorvastatin 40-80mg) is indicated for all patients with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, post-MI, post-stroke, and ACS. Moderate-intensity therapy (10-20mg) is indicated for primary prevention in diabetic patients aged 40-75 and patients with elevated 10-year ASCVD risk. Per ACC/AHA guidelines, atorvastatin 80mg should not be withheld in acute MI due to concerns about liver toxicity — the cardiovascular benefit is overwhelming. Pregnancy category X — absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy and lactation. Major interactions include strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin, itraconazole, HIV protease inhibitors) which dramatically increase statin levels and myopathy risk, cyclosporine, gemfibrozil (prefer fenofibrate if combination needed), and warfarin (may increase INR). The most common side effect is myalgia (5-10%) which is usually tolerable. Rhabdomyolysis is rare but potentially fatal — characterized by severe muscle pain, dark urine, and markedly elevated CK. Check CK only if symptomatic. New-onset diabetes is a class effect but cardiovascular benefit far outweighs this risk. No renal dose adjustment needed.

mechanism: Reduces hepatic glucose production, increases insulin sensitivity, decreases intestinal glucose absorption
standard_dosing: Start 500mg BID with meals, titrate to 1000mg BID over 4-8 weeks
renal_adjustment: eGFR 30-45: reduce to 500mg BID max; eGFR <30: contraindicated
hepatic_adjustment: Avoid in severe hepatic impairment (lactic acidosis risk)
major_interactions: Iodinated contrast dye (hold 48h before/after — lactic acidosis)
side_effects: GI upset (nausea, diarrhea, bloating — most common)
monitoring: eGFR annually; vitamin B12 every 2-3 years after 4 years of use; HbA1c every 3-6 months
content: Metformin (Glucophage) is a biguanide antidiabetic that reduces hepatic glucose production, increases peripheral insulin sensitivity, and decreases intestinal glucose absorption. It remains the undisputed first-line pharmacotherapy for Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus per ADA 2024 guidelines due to its efficacy, safety, low cost, weight neutrality, and potential cardiovascular benefit. Starting dose is 500mg twice daily with meals (to minimize GI side effects), titrated over 4-8 weeks to target of 1000mg twice daily. Extended-release formulation reduces GI side effects. Contraindicated when eGFR is below 30 mL/min (lactic acidosis risk), in metabolic acidosis, severe hepatic impairment, and active alcohol abuse. When eGFR is 30-45, reduce to maximum 500mg twice daily. A critical clinical pearl: hold metformin 48 hours before and after iodinated contrast dye administration due to risk of contrast-induced AKI worsening metformin accumulation and precipitating lactic acidosis. GI side effects (nausea, diarrhea, bloating, metallic taste) are the most common reason for discontinuation — mitigated by slow titration and taking with meals. Long-term B12 deficiency occurs in approximately 7% of patients on metformin for more than 4 years — check levels every 2-3 years. Lactic acidosis is extremely rare with appropriate patient selection. Metformin does not cause hypoglycemia when used as monotherapy. Weight neutral to mildly weight-reducing. Pregnancy category B.

generic_name: Insulin Regular (Humulin R / Novolin R) and Rapid-Acting (Lispro, Aspart, Glulisine)
mechanism: Binds insulin receptors, promoting cellular glucose uptake, glycogen synthesis, and inhibiting gluconeogenesis
standard_dosing: DKA: 0.1-0.14 units/kg/hr IV infusion; Hyperkalemia: 10 units IV with D50; SC: individualized
max_dose_per_day: No absolute maximum; titrated to glucose
renal_adjustment: Reduce dose (decreased insulin clearance in CKD/ESRD)
hepatic_adjustment: Reduce dose (decreased gluconeogenesis)
monitoring: Blood glucose (hourly in DKA, before meals/bedtime otherwise); potassium closely in DKA; HbA1c q3-6 months
content: Insulin (Regular and Rapid-Acting formulations) is a hormone that binds insulin receptors promoting cellular glucose uptake, glycogen synthesis, and inhibiting hepatic gluconeogenesis. It is essential for Type 1 diabetes, severe or uncontrolled Type 2 diabetes, diabetic ketoacidosis, hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state, and hyperkalemia management. In DKA, regular insulin is given as continuous IV infusion at 0.1-0.14 units/kg/hour — critically, do NOT start insulin until serum potassium is confirmed above 3.5 mEq/L, as insulin drives potassium intracellularly and can cause fatal hypokalemia. For hyperkalemia, 10 units regular insulin IV with 25g dextrose (D50) shifts potassium into cells, lowering serum K+ by 0.5-1.0 mEq/L within 15-30 minutes lasting 4-6 hours. Rapid-acting analogs (lispro, aspart, glulisine) have onset in 15 minutes and are used for mealtime coverage and correction doses. Hypoglycemia is the most dangerous side effect — symptoms include tremor, diaphoresis, confusion, seizures, and coma. Weight gain is common with insulin therapy. In CKD and ESRD, insulin clearance is reduced requiring dose reduction to prevent hypoglycemia. Beta-blockers mask adrenergic symptoms of hypoglycemia (tachycardia, tremor) making recognition difficult. Corticosteroids antagonize insulin action requiring higher doses. Always monitor potassium when using insulin for DKA or hyperkalemia treatment.

mechanism: Synthetic T4 that is converted to active T3 peripherally, restoring normal thyroid hormone levels
standard_dosing: 1.6 mcg/kg/day; elderly/cardiac: start 12.5-25 mcg/day; take on empty stomach 30-60 min before breakfast
renal_adjustment: No adjustment needed
hepatic_adjustment: No specific adjustment
major_interactions: Calcium/iron supplements (reduce absorption — separate by 4 hours)
Estrogen (may increase TBG, requiring dose increase)
monitoring: TSH in 6-8 weeks after initiation or dose change; annually once stable
content: Levothyroxine (Synthroid) is a synthetic thyroxine (T4) that serves as the standard treatment for hypothyroidism. T4 is converted to the active form T3 in peripheral tissues by deiodinase enzymes. Dosing is weight-based at approximately 1.6 mcg/kg/day for full replacement. In elderly patients and those with cardiac disease, start at very low doses (12.5-25 mcg/day) and increase by 12.5-25 mcg every 4-6 weeks to avoid precipitating angina or arrhythmias. Must be taken on an empty stomach 30-60 minutes before breakfast for optimal absorption. A critical contraindication is untreated adrenal insufficiency — starting levothyroxine without cortisol replacement can precipitate adrenal crisis by accelerating cortisol metabolism. Important absorption interactions: calcium and iron supplements reduce absorption and must be separated by at least 4 hours; PPIs and cholestyramine also interfere. Levothyroxine increases warfarin sensitivity by enhancing coagulation factor catabolism — monitor INR closely when initiating or adjusting thyroid replacement. Signs of over-replacement include tachycardia, palpitations, insomnia, weight loss, tremor, and anxiety. Long-term over-replacement with suppressed TSH increases risk of atrial fibrillation and osteoporosis, especially in postmenopausal women. Monitor TSH 6-8 weeks after any dose change and annually once stable. Pregnancy category A — safe and essential during pregnancy; increase dose by approximately 30% in pregnancy.

mechanism: Inhibits thyroid peroxidase, blocking iodine organification and thyroid hormone synthesis
standard_dosing: Initial: 10-30mg daily; Maintenance: 5-15mg daily; Thyroid storm: 20-40mg q4-6h
renal_adjustment: No specific adjustment
hepatic_adjustment: Caution; monitor LFTs
major_interactions: Warfarin (hyperthyroid state increases warfarin effect; as patient becomes euthyroid, warfarin needs increase)
monitoring: CBC with differential if fever/sore throat; LFTs; TFTs every 4-6 weeks until euthyroid
content: Methimazole is a thionamide antithyroid drug that inhibits thyroid peroxidase enzyme, blocking the organification of iodine and coupling of iodotyrosines, thereby reducing thyroid hormone synthesis. It is the preferred antithyroid drug for Graves disease and hyperthyroidism in all patients except during the first trimester of pregnancy (where PTU is preferred due to methimazole's teratogenic risk of aplasia cutis and choanal atresia). Initial dosing is 10-30mg daily depending on severity, with maintenance of 5-15mg daily once euthyroid. In thyroid storm, higher doses of 20-40mg every 4-6 hours are used. The most serious side effect is agranulocytosis (0.1-0.5%), which presents with fever and sore throat — patients must be instructed to immediately stop the medication and seek emergency care if they develop fever or pharyngitis. Obtain CBC with differential urgently if suspected. Hepatotoxicity occurs rarely and is typically cholestatic (unlike PTU which causes hepatocellular injury). A clinically important interaction involves warfarin: the hyperthyroid state increases sensitivity to warfarin, so as the patient becomes euthyroid on methimazole, warfarin doses may need to increase. Similarly, digoxin levels will rise as hyperthyroidism is controlled because digoxin clearance decreases. Monitor thyroid function tests every 4-6 weeks until euthyroid, then every 3 months. Methimazole has a longer half-life than PTU, allowing once-daily dosing which improves compliance.

mechanism: Blocks beta-1 and beta-2 adrenergic receptors; also inhibits peripheral conversion of T4 to T3
standard_dosing: Thyrotoxicosis: 20-40mg TID-QID; Migraine prophylaxis: 40-160mg daily; Variceal prophylaxis: titrate to HR 55-60
renal_adjustment: No adjustment needed
hepatic_adjustment: Reduce dose (extensive hepatic metabolism)
monitoring: Heart rate; blood pressure; respiratory status in patients with COPD
content: Propranolol is a non-selective beta-adrenergic blocker that blocks both beta-1 (cardiac) and beta-2 (bronchial, vascular) receptors. It has a unique role in thyrotoxicosis and thyroid storm because, in addition to controlling heart rate and tremor, it inhibits peripheral conversion of T4 to active T3, providing an antithyroid effect. Dosing for thyrotoxicosis is 20-40mg three to four times daily, titrated to control symptoms. Also widely used for essential tremor, performance anxiety, migraine prophylaxis (40-160mg daily), and portal hypertension variceal bleeding prophylaxis (titrate to target heart rate 55-60 bpm). Critically contraindicated in asthma and severe reactive airway disease because beta-2 blockade causes bronchospasm — this is a high-yield safety point. Also contraindicated in decompensated heart failure, severe bradycardia, and cocaine intoxication (beta-blockade with unopposed alpha-adrenergic stimulation can worsen hypertension and coronary vasospasm). Important interactions include calcium channel blockers (verapamil, diltiazem — risk of severe bradycardia and heart block), insulin and oral hypoglycemics (masks adrenergic hypoglycemia symptoms), and epinephrine (in anaphylaxis, beta-blocked patients may have refractory hypotension requiring glucagon). Due to non-selectivity, propranolol causes more bronchospasm, cold extremities, and fatigue than selective beta-1 blockers like metoprolol. Extensively hepatically metabolized — reduce dose in liver disease.

mechanism: Irreversibly inhibits H+/K+ ATPase (proton pump) in gastric parietal cells, suppressing acid secretion
standard_dosing: 20-40mg daily before breakfast; H. pylori: 20mg BID with antibiotics x14 days
renal_adjustment: No adjustment needed
hepatic_adjustment: Reduce dose in severe hepatic impairment
major_interactions: Clopidogrel (reduces activation via CYP2C19 — use pantoprazole instead)
monitoring: Magnesium if prolonged use; B12 if prolonged use; reassess PPI indication periodically
content: Omeprazole (Prilosec) is a proton pump inhibitor that irreversibly inhibits the H+/K+ ATPase proton pump in gastric parietal cells, providing the most potent suppression of gastric acid secretion available. Indicated for GERD, peptic ulcer disease, H. pylori eradication regimens, Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, and ICU stress ulcer prophylaxis. Standard dose is 20-40mg daily taken 30-60 minutes before breakfast for optimal efficacy. A critically important drug interaction is with clopidogrel: omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, the enzyme required to activate clopidogrel, significantly reducing its antiplatelet effect and increasing cardiovascular events. If a PPI is needed with clopidogrel, use pantoprazole which has minimal CYP2C19 inhibition. Long-term PPI use (beyond 8 weeks) carries several risks: increased C. difficile infection risk, hypomagnesemia, osteoporotic hip and vertebral fractures, vitamin B12 deficiency from impaired absorption, and fundic gland polyps. PPIs should be used at the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration necessary, with periodic reassessment of indication. Many patients are continued on PPIs long-term without clear indication. Other interactions include methotrexate (increased toxicity) and reduced absorption of calcium, iron, and B12 with chronic use.

mechanism: Amoxicillin inhibits cell wall synthesis; clavulanate inhibits beta-lactamase enzymes extending spectrum
standard_dosing: 875/125mg BID or 500/125mg TID; High-dose: 2000/125mg BID (resistant pneumococcus)
renal_adjustment: CrCl <30: 500/125mg BID; avoid 875mg formulation
hepatic_adjustment: Caution; monitor LFTs; avoid if prior cholestatic reaction
monitoring: LFTs if prolonged use; signs of hypersensitivity; renal function
content: Amoxicillin-Clavulanate (Augmentin) combines the aminopenicillin amoxicillin with the beta-lactamase inhibitor clavulanic acid, extending the antibacterial spectrum to include beta-lactamase-producing organisms such as H. influenzae, Moraxella catarrhalis, Staphylococcus aureus (MSSA), and anaerobes. This makes it a versatile outpatient antibiotic for sinusitis, otitis media, community-acquired pneumonia with comorbidities, UTIs, animal and human bite wounds (excellent anaerobic coverage for Pasteurella and Eikenella), aspiration pneumonia (anaerobic coverage), and skin and soft tissue infections. Standard dosing is 875/125mg twice daily. High-dose formulation (2000/125mg BID) is used for suspected resistant pneumococcus. Contraindicated in patients with penicillin anaphylaxis (type I hypersensitivity), prior cholestatic jaundice with this drug, and infectious mononucleosis (causes characteristic maculopapular rash). Diarrhea is the most common side effect and is primarily due to the clavulanate component — taking with food reduces this. Cholestatic hepatitis is a rare but important complication, more common in elderly patients and with prolonged courses. Renal adjustment needed when CrCl below 30: use 500/125mg BID and avoid the 875mg formulation. Interactions include warfarin (monitor INR), methotrexate (reduced renal excretion), and allopurinol (increased rash incidence). Cross-reactivity with cephalosporin allergy is approximately 1-2%. Pregnancy category B — widely used in pregnancy.

mechanism: Inhibits cell wall synthesis by binding D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of peptidoglycan precursors
contraindications: Oral form should not be used for systemic MRSA
standard_dosing: IV: 15-20mg/kg q8-12h (target trough 15-20 or AUC/MIC 400-600); Oral (C. diff): 125mg QID x10 days
route: IV (systemic), Oral (C. diff only — not absorbed systemically)
renal_adjustment: Dose by levels; extend interval in renal impairment; dialyzable
hepatic_adjustment: No specific adjustment
side_effects: Red man syndrome (histamine release — slow infusion rate)
monitoring: Trough levels (target 15-20 mcg/mL) or AUC-based dosing; serum creatinine; CBC
content: Vancomycin is a glycopeptide antibiotic that inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding to the D-Ala-D-Ala terminus of peptidoglycan precursors. It is the drug of choice for serious MRSA (methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus) infections and is used empirically in bacterial meningitis (with ceftriaxone), endocarditis, and as surgical prophylaxis in beta-lactam allergic patients. For systemic infections, IV vancomycin is dosed at 15-20mg/kg every 8-12 hours, guided by either trough-based monitoring (target 15-20 mcg/mL for serious infections) or the newer AUC/MIC-based dosing (target AUC 400-600). For C. difficile, oral vancomycin 125mg four times daily for 10 days is used — oral vancomycin is NOT absorbed systemically and acts locally in the GI tract, so it cannot be used for systemic MRSA infections. Red man syndrome is a histamine-mediated reaction (not true allergy) causing flushing, erythema, and pruritus of the upper body — prevented by slowing the infusion rate to over 60 minutes. Nephrotoxicity is the most clinically significant adverse effect, especially when combined with other nephrotoxins. The combination of vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam has been associated with significantly higher rates of AKI compared to vancomycin plus cefepime or meropenem. Other serious side effects include ototoxicity and drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS). Dose by drug levels and adjust for renal function.

mechanism: Piperacillin inhibits cell wall synthesis; tazobactam inhibits beta-lactamases
standard_dosing: 3.375g IV q6h (standard); 4.5g IV q6h (nosocomial pneumonia); Extended infusion: 4.5g over 4 hours q8h
renal_adjustment: CrCl 20-40: 2.25g q6h; CrCl <20: 2.25g q8h; HD: 2.25g q8h + extra dose after dialysis
hepatic_adjustment: No specific adjustment
monitoring: CBC (platelets); BMP (potassium); renal function; signs of hypersensitivity
content: Piperacillin-Tazobactam (Zosyn) is a broad-spectrum IV antibiotic combining the extended-spectrum penicillin piperacillin with the beta-lactamase inhibitor tazobactam. It provides coverage against gram-positives (streptococci, enterococci), gram-negatives (E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas aeruginosa), and anaerobes (Bacteroides fragilis), making it one of the most commonly used empiric antibiotics for sepsis. Per the Surviving Sepsis Campaign, vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam is a standard empiric regimen for sepsis. Standard dosing is 3.375g IV every 6 hours or 4.5g every 6 hours for nosocomial pneumonia. Extended infusion (4.5g over 4 hours every 8 hours) optimizes time above MIC and improves outcomes. A critical safety concern is the combination with vancomycin: studies have shown significantly increased rates of acute kidney injury compared to vancomycin plus cefepime or meropenem. Consider alternative gram-negative coverage if possible. Renal dose adjustment required: CrCl 20-40 mL/min use 2.25g every 6 hours. Notable for not covering MRSA (need vancomycin) and not covering atypical organisms. Notable side effects include thrombocytopenia, diarrhea, C. diff, hypokalemia, and rarely seizures at high doses. Do not mix with aminoglycosides in the same IV line (physical incompatibility). Pregnancy category B.

mechanism: Inhibits bacterial cell wall synthesis by binding penicillin-binding proteins (PBPs)
contraindications: Do not mix with calcium-containing solutions in neonates
standard_dosing: Pneumonia: 1g IV q24h; Meningitis: 2g IV q12h; Gonorrhea: 500mg IM x1; SBP prophylaxis: 1g IV q24h x7d
renal_adjustment: No adjustment needed (biliary excretion)
hepatic_adjustment: No specific adjustment unless combined renal+hepatic impairment
major_interactions: Calcium-containing IV solutions in neonates (fatal precipitates)
monitoring: Signs of hypersensitivity; C. diff if diarrhea; LFTs in prolonged use
content: Ceftriaxone (Rocephin) is a third-generation cephalosporin with broad gram-negative and moderate gram-positive activity. Its convenient once-daily dosing (due to long half-life of 6-9 hours), excellent CNS penetration, and biliary excretion make it one of the most versatile and commonly used parenteral antibiotics. Key indications include community-acquired pneumonia (1g IV daily with azithromycin), bacterial meningitis (2g IV every 12 hours with vancomycin), uncomplicated gonorrhea (500mg IM single dose), pyelonephritis, intra-abdominal infections, Lyme disease with CNS involvement, and spontaneous bacterial peritonitis prophylaxis during variceal bleeding (1g IV daily for 7 days). Does NOT cover MRSA, Pseudomonas, Enterococcus, or atypical organisms. No renal dose adjustment is needed because it is primarily excreted through the biliary system — a significant advantage. Cross-reactivity with penicillin allergy is approximately 1-2% (safe to use in patients with non-anaphylactic penicillin allergy). Critical safety concern in neonates: do not co-administer with calcium-containing IV solutions as fatal ceftriaxone-calcium precipitates can form in lungs and kidneys. A unique side effect is biliary sludging (pseudocholelithiasis) which can cause right upper quadrant pain mimicking cholecystitis — resolves after discontinuation. Can cause C. difficile colitis. Pregnancy category B.

mechanism: Binds 50S ribosomal subunit, inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis
contraindications: History of cholestatic jaundice with azithromycin
standard_dosing: CAP: 500mg day 1, then 250mg days 2-5; Z-pack: 250mg x6 over 5 days; Chlamydia: 1g single dose
renal_adjustment: No adjustment needed
hepatic_adjustment: Caution in hepatic impairment; avoid if prior cholestatic reaction
monitoring: ECG if QT risk factors; LFTs if symptoms; hearing if prolonged use
content: Azithromycin (Zithromax) is a macrolide antibiotic that binds the 50S ribosomal subunit, inhibiting bacterial protein synthesis. It provides excellent coverage of atypical organisms (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella) and is used in combination with ceftriaxone for inpatient community-acquired pneumonia. Its long tissue half-life (68 hours) allows short-course therapy — the classic Z-pack is 500mg on day 1 followed by 250mg on days 2-5. Also used for acute exacerbation of COPD with purulent sputum, chlamydia (1g single dose), and MAC prophylaxis in HIV patients. The most clinically significant safety concern is QT prolongation, which can cause torsades de pointes and sudden cardiac death — avoid in patients with known QT prolongation, on other QT-prolonging drugs (amiodarone, fluoroquinolones, antipsychotics), uncorrected hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia, or significant bradycardia. Other interactions include warfarin (monitor INR), digoxin (macrolides inhibit P-glycoprotein increasing digoxin levels — monitor digoxin levels), and cyclosporine. Unlike erythromycin and clarithromycin, azithromycin has minimal CYP3A4 inhibition, making it safer from a drug interaction standpoint. Side effects include GI disturbance (diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain), hepatotoxicity, and rare reversible hearing loss. No renal adjustment needed. Pregnancy category B.

drug_class: Vasopressor / Alpha-1 and Beta-1 Adrenergic Agonist
mechanism: Potent alpha-1 agonist causing vasoconstriction; moderate beta-1 agonist increasing cardiac contractility
contraindications: Hypovolemia without adequate fluid resuscitation first
standard_dosing: Start 0.1-0.5 mcg/kg/min; titrate to MAP >=65 mmHg; typical range 5-30 mcg/min
max_dose_per_day: No absolute max; titrate to effect (high doses suggest refractory shock)
route: IV (central line preferred; peripheral temporarily acceptable)
renal_adjustment: No specific adjustment
hepatic_adjustment: No specific adjustment
monitoring: Continuous arterial BP monitoring; MAP (target >=65); urine output; lactate clearance; peripheral perfusion
content: Norepinephrine (Levophed) is a potent vasopressor and the first-line agent for septic shock per the Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines. It acts primarily as an alpha-1 adrenergic agonist causing peripheral vasoconstriction to raise blood pressure, with moderate beta-1 agonist activity increasing cardiac contractility. Starting dose is 0.1-0.5 mcg/kg/min, titrated to target MAP of 65 mmHg or above. Typical dose range is 5-30 mcg/min. Administer through a central venous catheter whenever possible; peripheral IV access is acceptable temporarily but carries risk of severe tissue necrosis with extravasation — if extravasation occurs, infiltrate the area with phentolamine 5-10mg in 10mL normal saline. Should only be initiated after adequate fluid resuscitation (at least 30 mL/kg crystalloid in sepsis); using vasopressors without addressing hypovolemia worsens tissue perfusion. If MAP remains below 65 despite norepinephrine, add vasopressin 0.03 units/min as second-line (Surviving Sepsis Campaign recommendation). If norepinephrine requirements exceed 0.25 mcg/kg/min, consider adding hydrocortisone 200mg/day for refractory septic shock. Critical interactions include MAOIs (severe hypertensive crisis) and tricyclic antidepressants (potentiated effect). Monitoring requires continuous arterial blood pressure monitoring via arterial line, hourly urine output, lactate clearance every 2-6 hours, and assessment of peripheral perfusion (mottling, capillary refill).

mechanism: Converts plasminogen to plasmin, which degrades fibrin clots
standard_dosing: Stroke: 0.9mg/kg (max 90mg), 10% bolus + remainder over 60min; PE: 100mg over 2hr; STEMI: accelerated protocol
renal_adjustment: No specific adjustment
hepatic_adjustment: Increased bleeding risk in coagulopathy
major_interactions: No aspirin/anticoagulants for 24 hours post-stroke thrombolysis
side_effects: Hemorrhage (major risk — intracranial hemorrhage 6% in stroke)
monitoring: BP q15min during and 2hr post-infusion; neuro checks q15min (stroke); CT at 24hr post-stroke; signs of bleeding
content: Alteplase (Activase, tPA) is a thrombolytic agent that converts plasminogen to plasmin, which degrades fibrin clots and restores blood flow. It is a time-critical medication used in acute ischemic stroke, massive pulmonary embolism, and STEMI when PCI is not available. For acute ischemic stroke, alteplase 0.9mg/kg (maximum 90mg) is administered within 4.5 hours of symptom onset: 10% as IV bolus over 1 minute and the remainder infused over 60 minutes. Door-to-needle target is 60 minutes. Strict blood pressure control is required: BP must be below 185/110 before administration and below 180/105 for 24 hours after. No aspirin or anticoagulants for 24 hours post-stroke thrombolysis. For massive PE with hemodynamic instability, 100mg is infused over 2 hours. Contraindications include active internal bleeding, recent surgery within 14 days, prior intracranial hemorrhage, uncontrolled hypertension, platelets below 100,000, INR above 1.7, and blood glucose below 50 or above 400. The most feared complication is intracranial hemorrhage occurring in approximately 6% of stroke patients — but mortality benefit outweighs this risk in eligible patients. Angioedema occurs in 1-5%, especially in patients on ACE inhibitors. All anticoagulants and antiplatelets markedly increase bleeding risk. Post-thrombolysis monitoring includes BP every 15 minutes, frequent neurological assessments, and CT head at 24 hours to check for hemorrhagic transformation.

mechanism: Binds glucocorticoid receptors, suppressing inflammatory gene transcription and immune response
standard_dosing: Asthma/COPD: prednisone 40mg PO x5 days; Severe allergic: methylprednisolone 125mg IV; Autoimmune: variable
max_dose_per_day: Variable by indication (pulse therapy up to 1g methylprednisolone)
renal_adjustment: No specific adjustment
hepatic_adjustment: Prednisone requires hepatic conversion to prednisolone; use prednisolone in severe liver disease
monitoring: Blood glucose; BP; bone density if prolonged; potassium; signs of infection; adrenal function if tapering
content: Prednisone (oral) and Methylprednisolone (IV Solu-Medrol) are systemic corticosteroids that bind glucocorticoid receptors, suppressing inflammatory gene transcription and broadly suppressing the immune response. They are among the most widely used anti-inflammatory and immunosuppressive agents in medicine. Key indications include asthma exacerbation (prednisone 40mg daily for 5 days — no taper needed for short courses), COPD exacerbation (prednisone 40mg for 5 days), autoimmune diseases (SLE, RA, vasculitis), severe allergic reactions and anaphylaxis prevention of biphasic reaction (methylprednisolone 125mg IV), gout flare (if NSAIDs contraindicated), bacterial meningitis adjunct (dexamethasone preferred), and organ transplant rejection. Short courses (5-7 days) generally do not require tapering. Prolonged courses exceeding 2-3 weeks suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis and require gradual tapering to avoid adrenal crisis. Major side effects with chronic use include hyperglycemia (steroid-induced diabetes), immunosuppression with increased infection risk, osteoporosis, adrenal suppression, weight gain with Cushingoid features, hypertension, mood changes including psychosis, GI ulceration (especially with concurrent NSAIDs), cataracts and glaucoma, and skin thinning. Fluoroquinolones combined with corticosteroids increase tendon rupture risk. Prednisone is a prodrug requiring hepatic conversion to prednisolone — in severe liver disease, use prednisolone directly. During illness or surgery, patients on chronic steroids need stress-dose steroids to prevent adrenal crisis.

mechanism: Selectively inhibits serotonin reuptake in the synaptic cleft, increasing serotonergic neurotransmission
standard_dosing: Depression: start 50mg daily, titrate by 25-50mg every 1-2 weeks; Max: 200mg daily
renal_adjustment: No adjustment needed
hepatic_adjustment: Reduce dose in hepatic impairment; use lower starting dose
monitoring: PHQ-9 at 2, 4, 8 weeks then monthly; suicidality in under-25s; sodium in elderly; sexual dysfunction screening
content: Sertraline (Zoloft) is a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor (SSRI) that blocks serotonin reuptake in the synaptic cleft, increasing serotonergic neurotransmission. It is one of the most commonly prescribed first-line antidepressants for major depressive disorder, and is preferred for patients with cardiac disease due to its favorable cardiovascular safety profile (SADHART trial). Also indicated for generalized anxiety, panic disorder, PTSD, OCD, social anxiety, and premenstrual dysphoric disorder. Starting dose is 50mg daily, titrated by 25-50mg every 1-2 weeks to a maximum of 200mg daily. Allow 4-6 weeks for adequate therapeutic trial before switching. The most dangerous interaction is with MAOIs — concurrent use within 14 days can cause serotonin syndrome (hyperthermia, rigidity, myoclonus, autonomic instability, mental status changes) which is potentially fatal. Other serotonergic drugs (triptans, tramadol, linezolid, methylene blue) also increase risk. Sertraline combined with NSAIDs, aspirin, or warfarin increases GI bleeding risk due to serotonin's role in platelet aggregation. SSRIs carry an FDA Black Box Warning for increased suicidality in patients under 25 — monitor weekly for the first 4 weeks. Common side effects include nausea (most common initial complaint, usually resolves), diarrhea, sexual dysfunction (30-40%), insomnia, and weight gain with long-term use. Hyponatremia from SIADH can occur especially in elderly patients — check sodium if confusion develops. Gradual tapering is required to prevent discontinuation syndrome.

mechanism: Most selective SSRI; inhibits serotonin reuptake transporter with minimal off-target receptor activity
standard_dosing: Start 10mg daily; may increase to 20mg after 1 week if needed
renal_adjustment: No adjustment for mild-moderate; caution in severe
hepatic_adjustment: Max 10mg daily in hepatic impairment
monitoring: PHQ-9; suicidality in under-25s; ECG if QT risk; sodium in elderly
content: Escitalopram (Lexapro) is the S-enantiomer of citalopram and the most selective SSRI available, with minimal off-target receptor activity translating to fewer side effects and drug interactions compared to other SSRIs. It is a first-line treatment for major depressive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder. Starting dose is 10mg daily, which can be increased to 20mg after at least 1 week. Maximum dose is 20mg daily, reduced to 10mg in elderly patients and those with hepatic impairment. A unique safety concern compared to sertraline is dose-dependent QT prolongation — do not exceed 20mg daily and avoid combining with other QT-prolonging drugs (amiodarone, fluoroquinolones, antipsychotics, ondansetron). As with all SSRIs, the most dangerous interaction is with MAOIs causing potentially fatal serotonin syndrome — require 14-day washout. FDA Black Box Warning for increased suicidality in patients under 25 applies. Common side effects include nausea, insomnia, sexual dysfunction, headache, and somnolence. Hyponatremia from SIADH is a concern especially in elderly patients. Escitalopram is often preferred over citalopram because it achieves the same efficacy at half the dose with less QT prolongation risk. The clean pharmacokinetic profile with minimal CYP enzyme interactions makes it a good choice for patients on multiple medications. Taper gradually to prevent discontinuation syndrome.

mechanism: Modulates intracellular signaling pathways including inositol phosphate and GSK-3beta; exact mechanism incompletely understood
standard_dosing: Start 300mg BID-TID; target serum level 0.6-1.2 mEq/L (acute mania: 0.8-1.2; maintenance: 0.6-0.8)
renal_adjustment: Reduce dose; avoid in severe renal impairment; renally cleared
hepatic_adjustment: No specific adjustment (not hepatically metabolized)
major_interactions: NSAIDs (increase lithium levels by reducing renal clearance)
monitoring: Serum lithium levels (q5-7 days until stable, then q3-6 months); TSH and renal function q6-12 months; calcium annually
content: Lithium is the gold-standard mood stabilizer for bipolar disorder and the only psychiatric medication proven to reduce suicide risk. Its mechanism involves modulation of intracellular signaling pathways including inositol phosphate turnover and GSK-3beta inhibition, though the exact mechanism remains incompletely understood. Used for acute mania, bipolar maintenance, bipolar depression augmentation, and treatment-resistant unipolar depression augmentation. Dosing is guided by serum levels: target 0.8-1.2 mEq/L for acute mania and 0.6-0.8 mEq/L for maintenance. Draw trough levels 12 hours post-dose. Lithium has a very narrow therapeutic index — toxicity occurs at levels above 1.5 mEq/L and is life-threatening above 2.5 mEq/L (coarse tremor, confusion, seizures, cardiac arrhythmias). The most clinically important drug interactions involve drugs that reduce renal lithium clearance, causing toxicity: NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors, ARBs, and thiazide diuretics all increase lithium levels dangerously. Patients must maintain consistent sodium and fluid intake — dehydration concentrates lithium. Long-term side effects include nephrogenic diabetes insipidus (polyuria, polydipsia), hypothyroidism (check TSH every 6-12 months), chronic renal impairment, fine tremor, weight gain, cognitive dulling, and GI upset. Pregnancy category D — lithium causes Ebstein anomaly (tricuspid valve malformation) though the absolute risk is lower than historically reported (0.05-0.1%). Renal function and TSH must be monitored regularly.

mechanism: Increases GABA levels, blocks voltage-gated sodium channels, modulates T-type calcium channels
standard_dosing: Seizures: 10-15mg/kg/day in divided doses, titrate to levels; Mania: 750mg/day in divided doses; Target level: 50-100 mcg/mL
renal_adjustment: No specific adjustment; free levels may be elevated
hepatic_adjustment: Contraindicated in significant hepatic disease
monitoring: Serum levels (50-100 mcg/mL); LFTs; CBC (platelets); ammonia if altered mental status
content: Valproic Acid (Depakene/Depakote) is an anticonvulsant and mood stabilizer that works through multiple mechanisms: increasing GABA levels, blocking voltage-gated sodium channels, and modulating T-type calcium channels. It is effective for both generalized and focal seizures, acute mania in bipolar disorder, and migraine prophylaxis. Target therapeutic level is 50-100 mcg/mL. Pregnancy category X — valproate is the most teratogenic commonly used anticonvulsant, causing neural tube defects (spina bifida) in 1-2% of exposed fetuses and dose-dependent cognitive impairment in children. Must be avoided in women of childbearing potential when alternatives exist. A critical drug interaction is with carbapenems (meropenem, ertapenem) which dramatically reduce valproate levels by up to 60-80% within 24 hours — this combination is essentially contraindicated. Valproate doubles lamotrigine levels (reduce lamotrigine dose by 50% when adding valproate). Serious side effects include fatal hepatotoxicity (highest risk in children under 2 on polytherapy), acute pancreatitis, dose-related thrombocytopenia, weight gain, tremor, alopecia, and hyperammonemia (can cause encephalopathy even with normal valproate levels — check ammonia if altered mental status). Metabolized hepatically; contraindicated in significant liver disease and urea cycle disorders. Screen for POLG mitochondrial mutations before use as valproate can cause fatal hepatotoxicity in these patients.

mechanism: Binds synaptic vesicle protein SV2A, modulating neurotransmitter release
standard_dosing: Start 500mg BID, increase by 500mg every 2 weeks to 1000-1500mg BID; IV: same doses
renal_adjustment: CrCl 30-50: 500-1000mg BID; CrCl <30: 250-750mg BID; HD: supplement after dialysis
hepatic_adjustment: No adjustment needed (renally cleared)
monitoring: Mood and behavior changes; renal function for dose adjustment; no routine level monitoring needed
content: Levetiracetam (Keppra) is an anticonvulsant that binds synaptic vesicle protein SV2A, modulating neurotransmitter release. It is one of the most widely prescribed anticonvulsants due to its broad spectrum efficacy, minimal drug interactions, availability of IV formulation, and no need for therapeutic drug level monitoring. Indicated for focal seizures, generalized tonic-clonic seizures, myoclonic seizures, IV status epilepticus, and seizure prophylaxis in neurosurgery and traumatic brain injury. Start at 500mg twice daily, increasing by 500mg every 2 weeks to target 1000-1500mg twice daily. The minimal drug interaction profile is a major clinical advantage — levetiracetam does not induce or inhibit hepatic CYP enzymes, making it safe to combine with other medications in complex patients. It is renally cleared, requiring dose reduction in renal impairment (CrCl below 50) with supplemental dosing after hemodialysis. No hepatic adjustment needed. The most clinically significant side effect is behavioral and psychiatric disturbance: irritability, aggression, agitation, and depression occurring in 5-15% of patients — this can be dose-limiting and may require switching to an alternative anticonvulsant. Other side effects include somnolence, dizziness, fatigue, and headache. Pyridoxine (vitamin B6) supplementation may reduce behavioral side effects. Pregnancy category C — generally considered one of the safer anticonvulsants in pregnancy based on registry data.

mechanism: Enhances GABA-A receptor activity, increasing chloride conductance and neuronal inhibition
standard_dosing: Anxiety: 0.5-2mg PO q8h PRN; Alcohol withdrawal: per CIWA protocol; Status epilepticus: 4mg IV (0.1mg/kg)
renal_adjustment: No adjustment needed
hepatic_adjustment: PREFERRED benzodiazepine in liver disease (no active metabolites, conjugation metabolism only)
major_interactions: Opioids (additive respiratory depression — FDA boxed warning)
monitoring: Respiratory rate and sedation level; CIWA score in alcohol withdrawal; fall risk in elderly
content: Lorazepam (Ativan) is an intermediate-acting benzodiazepine that enhances GABA-A receptor activity, increasing chloride ion conductance and neuronal inhibition throughout the CNS. It is the preferred benzodiazepine in patients with hepatic disease because it is metabolized by glucuronidation (conjugation) only, producing no active metabolites — unlike diazepam and chlordiazepoxide which undergo extensive hepatic oxidative metabolism. First-line for status epilepticus at 4mg IV (0.1mg/kg), and widely used for alcohol withdrawal (per CIWA-Ar protocol: administer 2-4mg IV/PO when CIWA score exceeds 8-10), acute anxiety and agitation, procedural sedation, and chemotherapy-induced nausea. The most critical safety concern is respiratory depression, especially when combined with opioids — an FDA Boxed Warning exists for the concurrent use of benzodiazepines and opioids due to risk of respiratory arrest and death. Alcohol combined with lorazepam is similarly dangerous. Other side effects include sedation, paradoxical agitation (especially in elderly — use with caution), physical dependence with withdrawal syndrome (seizures, delirium) after prolonged use, anterograde amnesia, ataxia, and falls in elderly patients. For alcohol withdrawal, symptom-triggered dosing per CIWA protocol is superior to fixed-schedule dosing, resulting in less total medication use and shorter treatment duration. In delirium tremens, very high doses may be required — refractory cases may need phenobarbital or propofol. Schedule IV controlled substance. Pregnancy category D.

mechanism: Inhibits dihydrofolate reductase (DHFR), reducing DNA synthesis and cell proliferation; also has anti-inflammatory effects at low doses.
standard_dosing: RA: 7.5-25mg PO/SC once weekly; always supplement with folic acid 1mg daily to reduce toxicity
max_dose_per_day: 25mg/week (RA); higher doses used in chemotherapy protocols
renal_adjustment: Avoid if CrCl <30 mL/min; reduce dose for CrCl 30-50 mL/min; renally cleared
hepatic_adjustment: Avoid in significant hepatic disease; hepatotoxic — monitor LFTs
major_interactions: NSAIDs (increased methotrexate toxicity — reduce renal clearance)
monitoring: CBC with differential; LFTs; creatinine — at baseline then monthly x3 months then q8-12 weeks; consider liver biopsy after cumulative dose 3.5-4g
content: Methotrexate (MTX) is the anchor disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD) for rheumatoid arthritis and is also widely used in psoriasis, psoriatic arthritis, and inflammatory myopathies. At low weekly doses used in rheumatology, its primary mechanism is anti-inflammatory via adenosine release rather than pure DHFR inhibition. It is dosed once weekly (not daily) in rheumatic diseases — a critical prescribing point — typically at 7.5mg weekly titrated to 15-25mg weekly based on response, given orally or subcutaneously (SC has better bioavailability). Folic acid 1mg daily must always be co-prescribed to reduce mucositis, hepatotoxicity, and nausea without compromising efficacy. Major toxicities include hepatotoxicity (cumulative dose-dependent fibrosis), myelosuppression, mucositis, and pulmonary toxicity (methotrexate pneumonitis — presents with dry cough, dyspnea, and fever, requiring immediate drug discontinuation). Methotrexate is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy (Category X — major teratogen causing neural tube defects and embryotoxicity) and must be discontinued at least 3 months before planned conception in both men and women. NSAIDs reduce renal clearance of methotrexate and dramatically increase toxicity — this combination must be used with extreme caution. TMP-SMX is contraindicated concurrently due to additive folate antagonism causing severe pancytopenia. Monitoring includes monthly CBC and LFTs for the first 3 months, then every 8-12 weeks once stable. Creatinine must also be monitored as renal impairment reduces clearance. Live vaccines are absolutely contraindicated in patients on methotrexate. Despite its toxicity profile, methotrexate remains the most cost-effective and widely validated DMARD for RA with over 50 years of clinical experience.

mechanism: Inhibits lysosomal toll-like receptor activation and antigen presentation; reduces pro-inflammatory cytokine production.
standard_dosing: 200-400mg PO daily; weight-based max 5mg/kg/day to reduce retinal toxicity risk
renal_adjustment: Use with caution in severe renal impairment; reduce dose
hepatic_adjustment: Use with caution in hepatic disease
major_interactions: QT-prolonging drugs (additive QT prolongation — azithromycin, fluoroquinolones)
side_effects: Retinal toxicity (maculopathy — dose and duration dependent)
monitoring: Annual ophthalmologic exam (baseline then yearly after 5 years of use, or earlier if risk factors); ECG baseline; G6PD before starting
pregnancy_category: C (considered safe in pregnancy for SLE — benefit outweighs risk)
content: Hydroxychloroquine (HCQ, Plaquenil) is an antimalarial agent with well-established immunomodulatory properties, recommended for ALL patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) regardless of disease severity due to its ability to reduce flares, organ damage accrual, and mortality. In rheumatoid arthritis, it is used as monotherapy for mild disease or in combination with methotrexate and sulfasalazine (triple therapy). It is considered one of the safest DMARDs and is among the few rheumatologic medications that can be continued throughout pregnancy in SLE, where it actually reduces neonatal lupus risk. The most important and feared toxicity is irreversible retinal toxicity (hydroxychloroquine maculopathy) causing bull's-eye maculopathy and permanent vision loss. Risk is related to cumulative dose and daily dose exceeding 5mg/kg/day — annual ophthalmologic screening with OCT and visual field testing is mandatory after 5 years of use (or earlier in high-risk patients). QT prolongation is a concern, particularly when combined with azithromycin or fluoroquinolones. GI side effects (nausea, abdominal discomfort) are common early but typically resolve — taking with food reduces symptoms. HCQ has a very long half-life of approximately 40-50 days, meaning it takes months to reach steady state and months to fully leave the body after discontinuation. It also has favorable effects on lipid profiles and glucose metabolism, providing cardiovascular benefits in SLE patients. Unlike many immunosuppressants, HCQ does not significantly increase infection risk, making it uniquely safe.

mechanism: Binds tubulin, inhibiting microtubule polymerization and disrupting neutrophil migration and activation; reduces MSU crystal-mediated inflammation.
indications: Gout prophylaxis during urate-lowering therapy initiation
contraindications: Severe renal impairment with concurrent strong CYP3A4 or P-gp inhibitors
Severe hepatic impairment combined with renal impairment
standard_dosing: Acute gout: 1.2mg PO then 0.6mg 1 hour later; Prophylaxis: 0.6mg once or twice daily; Pericarditis: 0.5mg BID
max_dose_per_day: 1.8mg for acute gout (low-dose regimen); 1.2mg/day for prophylaxis
renal_adjustment: Reduce dose in moderate-severe renal impairment (CrCl <30); avoid with CYP3A4 inhibitors if CrCl <30
hepatic_adjustment: Use with caution in severe hepatic impairment
major_interactions: Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (clarithromycin, cyclosporine, itraconazole — dramatically increase colchicine levels; potentially fatal toxicity)
monitoring: CBC and renal/hepatic function periodically; watch for toxicity symptoms (GI then neuromuscular then multi-organ failure in severe overdose)
content: Colchicine is a first-line agent for acute gout flares and pericarditis, working by disrupting neutrophil microtubule function and inhibiting NLRP3 inflammasome activation, thereby reducing crystal-induced and pericardial inflammation. For acute gout, the modern low-dose regimen (1.2mg followed by 0.6mg one hour later) is as effective as the traditional high-dose approach with dramatically fewer GI side effects — diarrhea was the limiting toxicity with older high-dose protocols. The low-dose regimen must be started within 36 hours of flare onset for maximum efficacy. For pericarditis, colchicine 0.5mg twice daily added to aspirin significantly reduces recurrence (COPE and ICAP trials). For gout prophylaxis during allopurinol initiation, 0.6mg once or twice daily prevents mobilization flares for the first 3-6 months of urate-lowering therapy. The most critical drug interaction is with strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (particularly clarithromycin and cyclosporine) and P-glycoprotein inhibitors, which can cause severe, potentially fatal colchicine toxicity manifesting as multi-organ failure, neuromuscular toxicity, and bone marrow suppression. Dose must be significantly reduced or the drug avoided entirely when these combinations are necessary. Colchicine is renally cleared and dose adjustment is required in renal impairment. The GI side effect of diarrhea is a useful pharmacodynamic endpoint — if diarrhea occurs before pain relief, the maximum tolerable dose has been reached. Colchicine is safe in patients with G6PD deficiency unlike some other gout treatments.

mechanism: Inhibits xanthine oxidase, reducing conversion of hypoxanthine and xanthine to uric acid, lowering serum urate levels.
contraindications: Acute gout flare (do not initiate during flare)
Hypersensitivity (severe reactions — HLA-B*58:01 testing in high-risk populations)
Concurrent azathioprine or 6-mercaptopurine without dose reduction
standard_dosing: Start 100mg PO daily; titrate by 100mg every 2-4 weeks to target uric acid <6 mg/dL; typical maintenance 300mg daily
renal_adjustment: Major reduction in CKD: CrCl 10-50 mL/min start 50-100mg daily; CrCl <10 use 100mg every 2-3 days
hepatic_adjustment: Use with caution
major_interactions: Azathioprine/6-mercaptopurine (CRITICAL — inhibits their metabolism via xanthine oxidase; reduce dose 75% or avoid)
side_effects: Allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (AHS — rare but life-threatening: fever, rash, eosinophilia, hepatitis, renal failure)
monitoring: Serum uric acid (target <6 mg/dL; <5 mg/dL if tophi present); LFTs and CBC; renal function; HLA-B*58:01 testing recommended in Han Chinese, Thai, Korean patients before starting
content: Allopurinol is the most commonly used urate-lowering therapy (ULT) for chronic gout and is first-line per ACR guidelines. It must never be started during an acute gout flare, as mobilization of urate crystals during initiation can worsen or prolong the attack — always start after the acute flare has fully resolved, with colchicine or NSAID prophylaxis covering the first 3-6 months of ULT. The critical principle is start low and titrate slowly: begin at 100mg daily (50mg daily in moderate-severe CKD) and increase every 2-4 weeks until serum uric acid falls below 6 mg/dL (below 5 mg/dL if tophi are present). The most dangerous toxicity is allopurinol hypersensitivity syndrome (AHS), a severe cutaneous adverse reaction including Stevens-Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis, strongly associated with the HLA-B*58:01 allele found at high frequency in Han Chinese (6-8%), Thai (6-8%), and Korean (12%) populations — genetic testing before initiation is recommended in these groups and required before use in some Asian countries. The interaction with azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine is critically important: allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase which metabolizes these drugs, causing potentially fatal accumulation — if combination is unavoidable, reduce azathioprine/6-MP dose by 75% with close CBC monitoring. Thiazide diuretics and renal impairment increase allopurinol toxicity risk. Febuxostat is an alternative xanthine oxidase inhibitor for patients intolerant of allopurinol, though it has an FDA warning for cardiovascular mortality and should not be used in patients with established cardiovascular disease.

drug_class: Non-Steroidal Anti-Inflammatory Drug (NSAID) / COX-1 and COX-2 Inhibitor
mechanism: Inhibits COX-1 and COX-2, reducing prostaglandin synthesis, thereby decreasing inflammation, pain, and fever.
indications: Patent ductus arteriosus closure (IV in neonates)
contraindications: Active peptic ulcer disease or GI bleeding
standard_dosing: Acute gout: 50mg PO TID for 3-5 days then taper; Ankylosing spondylitis: 25-50mg TID
renal_adjustment: Avoid in severe renal impairment (CrCl <30); use with caution and at lowest effective dose in mild-moderate CKD
hepatic_adjustment: Use with caution in hepatic disease
major_interactions: ACE inhibitors/ARBs (reduced antihypertensive effect; acute kidney injury — triple whammy with diuretics)
Methotrexate (reduced renal clearance — increased MTX toxicity)
side_effects: GI ulceration and bleeding (highest GI risk of all NSAIDs)
Cardiovascular events (MI, stroke with long-term use)
monitoring: Renal function; BP; signs of GI bleeding (stool guaiac); CBC with long-term use; consider PPI co-prescription for GI protection
content: Indomethacin is one of the most potent non-selective NSAIDs and is classically considered first-line for acute gout flares at 50mg three times daily, though modern guidelines recognize colchicine and other NSAIDs as equally effective alternatives with better tolerability. It is also highly effective for ankylosing spondylitis and is used IV in neonates to close a hemodynamically significant patent ductus arteriosus. For acute gout, the full anti-inflammatory dose (50mg TID) is used for the first 2-3 days, then tapered as inflammation resolves, typically over 5-7 days total. Indomethacin has among the highest GI toxicity rates of all NSAIDs due to its potent COX-1 inhibition affecting gastric mucosal prostaglandins — always prescribe with a proton pump inhibitor if treatment exceeds a few days or if the patient has GI risk factors. The triple whammy combination (NSAID + ACE inhibitor/ARB + diuretic) is particularly dangerous and a common cause of hospital-acquired acute kidney injury. The methotrexate interaction is critically important — NSAIDs reduce renal tubular secretion of methotrexate, dramatically increasing methotrexate plasma levels and toxicity risk, particularly in patients on weekly methotrexate for RA. Indomethacin is contraindicated in the third trimester of pregnancy as it can cause premature closure of the ductus arteriosus and fetal renal dysfunction. Compared to other NSAIDs, indomethacin has more CNS side effects including headache, dizziness, and confusion, especially in the elderly. Long-term use carries increased cardiovascular risk (MI, stroke) as with all non-selective NSAIDs.

drug_class: Sympathomimetic / Catecholamine / Alpha and Beta Agonist
mechanism: Agonist of alpha-1 (vasoconstriction), alpha-2, beta-1 (increased HR and contractility), beta-2 (bronchodilation) receptors; stabilizes mast cells and reverses anaphylaxis pathophysiology.
indications: Anaphylaxis (FIRST LINE — no contraindications in anaphylaxis)
contraindications: No absolute contraindications in anaphylaxis or cardiac arrest
Relative: hypertension, coronary artery disease, hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma (for elective/non-emergency use)
standard_dosing: Anaphylaxis: 0.3-0.5mg IM (1:1000) into anterolateral thigh; repeat q5-15 min if needed; Cardiac arrest: 1mg IV q3-5 min
max_dose_per_day: Titrated to clinical response; no fixed maximum in emergency settings
route: IM (anaphylaxis — preferred), IV (cardiac arrest, vasopressor infusion), Subcutaneous, Nebulized, Endotracheal
renal_adjustment: No specific adjustment; use clinically guided
hepatic_adjustment: No specific adjustment
major_interactions: Beta-blockers (epinephrine less effective; may cause paradoxical hypertension from unopposed alpha — use glucagon)
monitoring: Continuous ECG and BP monitoring during IV infusion; site inspection for extravasation; SpO2; clinical response to anaphylaxis symptoms
content: Epinephrine is the single most important medication in emergency medicine and is the absolute first-line treatment for anaphylaxis — there is NO contraindication to epinephrine in anaphylaxis, and delay in administration is the primary cause of anaphylaxis deaths. For anaphylaxis, it must be administered intramuscularly into the anterolateral thigh at 0.3-0.5mg (1:1000 concentration = 1mg/mL), which provides faster and more reliable absorption than the subcutaneous route. The IM thigh route achieves peak plasma levels significantly faster than deltoid injection. The auto-injector devices (EpiPen) deliver 0.3mg (adult) or 0.15mg (pediatric) and should always be prescribed in pairs at discharge from any anaphylaxis visit. All other treatments in anaphylaxis — antihistamines, corticosteroids, bronchodilators — are adjuncts and should never delay epinephrine administration. Antihistamines (diphenhydramine) do NOT treat life-threatening anaphylaxis features (hypotension, laryngeal edema, bronchospasm) and are not a substitute for epinephrine. In patients on beta-blockers who fail to respond to epinephrine, glucagon 1mg IV is the treatment of choice as it bypasses beta-receptor blockade. For cardiac arrest (ACLS), 1mg IV every 3-5 minutes improves return of spontaneous circulation. As a vasopressor infusion, epinephrine is used when norepinephrine is insufficient, providing additional beta-1 inotropic support. Racemic epinephrine nebulization treats croup by reducing subglottic edema through alpha-mediated vasoconstriction — patients require 2-4 hours of observation for rebound edema.

mechanism: Selectively stimulates beta-2 adrenergic receptors in bronchial smooth muscle, causing bronchodilation via cAMP-mediated relaxation. Also shifts potassium intracellularly via Na+/K+-ATPase activation.
indications: Hyperkalemia (nebulized as adjunct — shifts K+ intracellularly)
standard_dosing: Acute asthma: 2.5mg nebulized q20 min x3 doses then q1-4h; MDI: 4-8 puffs q20 min x3 then q1-4h; Hyperkalemia: 10-20mg nebulized over 15 min
max_dose_per_day: Continuous nebulization in acute severe asthma; otherwise guided by clinical response
route: Inhaled (nebulization, MDI), IV (not available in US)
renal_adjustment: No adjustment needed
hepatic_adjustment: No adjustment needed
major_interactions: Beta-blockers (antagonize bronchodilation — avoid non-selective beta-blockers in asthma)
Digoxin (hypokalemia from albuterol increases digoxin toxicity)
Other sympathomimetics (additive tachycardia and cardiovascular effects)
side_effects: Hypokalemia (especially with high doses — important in hyperkalemia management)
monitoring: HR; SpO2; peak expiratory flow or FEV1; potassium if high doses used for hyperkalemia; blood glucose in diabetics
content: Albuterol (salbutamol) is the most widely used short-acting beta-2 agonist (SABA) and is the cornerstone of acute asthma and COPD exacerbation treatment.
