A continuous infusion of 1-2mg/min is an alternative for more gradual control. Labetalol is a first-line agent for aortic dissection — in Type B dissection management, the goal is to simultaneously reduce heart rate (reducing shear force from cardiac impulse) and mean arterial pressure, which labetalol achieves with a single agent. IV labetalol is also the preferred antihypertensive in obstetric emergencies (severe hypertension in pre-eclampsia) along with IV hydralazine and oral nifedipine — it is safe in pregnancy and well-established in obstetric practice. The absolute contraindications in asthma and COPD with bronchospasm are critical — beta-2 receptor blockade can cause life-threatening bronchospasm in these patients, and nicardipine should be used instead. The scalp tingling sensation is a distinctive and harmless side effect reported by many patients receiving IV labetalol, useful for confirming adequate drug delivery. Patients must remain supine during IV administration to prevent orthostatic hypotension. In cocaine-induced hypertensive emergency, labetalol as the sole agent may be relatively contraindicated due to theoretical concern of unopposed alpha stimulation — though clinical evidence is mixed; phentolamine (alpha blocker) or benzodiazepines are often preferred.

mechanism: Provides calcium ions that directly antagonize the cardiac membrane-depolarizing effects of hyperkalemia by raising the threshold potential of cardiac cell membranes, increasing the difference between resting and threshold potential; restores normal cardiac membrane excitability without lowering serum potassium. Also used for calcium replacement in hypocalcemia.
indications: Hyperkalemia with ECG changes (cardioprotection — FIRST and most urgent measure)
contraindications: Digoxin toxicity (calcium potentiates digoxin toxicity — use with extreme caution if absolutely necessary)
standard_dosing: Hyperkalemia: 1g (10mL of 10% calcium gluconate) IV over 2-3 minutes; may repeat in 5 minutes if ECG changes persist; Hypocalcemia: 1-2g IV over 10-20 minutes
max_dose_per_day: Individualized — guided by ECG response and serum calcium levels
renal_adjustment: Use with caution in renal failure; risk of metastatic calcium-phosphate calcification in hyperphosphatemic patients; dialysis patients require close monitoring
hepatic_adjustment: No specific adjustment
major_interactions: Digoxin (CRITICAL — calcium potentiates digoxin toxicity and can trigger fatal arrhythmias; if must be given in digoxin-toxic patients, administer very slowly over 20-30 minutes with continuous ECG monitoring)
Calcium channel blockers (calcium antagonizes their pharmacologic vasodilatory effect — used therapeutically in CCB overdose)
Ceftriaxone (precipitates in IV tubing as calcium-ceftriaxone salt — flush line thoroughly between administrations; NEVER co-infuse in neonates)
side_effects: Bradycardia (if infused too rapidly — reduce infusion rate immediately)
Tissue necrosis and skin sloughing (extravasation — calcium gluconate is less caustic than calcium chloride but extravasation still requires prompt treatment)
monitoring: Continuous ECG during IV administration (watch for bradycardia, QT shortening); serum calcium; HR and BP; IV site for extravasation; serum potassium to assess whether definitive potassium-lowering therapy is working
content: Calcium gluconate is the most critical FIRST intervention in hyperkalemia with ECG changes, because it works within minutes to stabilize the cardiac membrane and prevent fatal arrhythmias — it is the only treatment that directly protects the heart while other therapies work to lower potassium levels. Importantly, calcium gluconate does NOT lower serum potassium — it solely stabilizes the cardiac membrane by raising the threshold potential. After administering calcium gluconate, definitive potassium-lowering therapy (insulin-glucose, albuterol, kayexalate, furosemide, or dialysis) must be initiated immediately. The ECG serves as a real-time guide to treatment: if peaked T waves are the only finding, the urgency is high but slightly less immediate; if P waves are disappearing, QRS is widening, or a sine wave pattern is developing, calcium gluconate must be given immediately and emergent dialysis arranged. One gram (10mL of 10% solution) is given over 2-3 minutes; if ECG changes persist after 5 minutes, a second gram is given. The effect lasts only 30-60 minutes — calcium gluconate is a bridge, not a definitive treatment. Calcium gluconate is preferred over calcium chloride in peripheral IV lines because calcium chloride is more caustic and causes severe tissue necrosis if it extravasates — calcium chloride is reserved for central venous access or cardiac arrest situations where faster onset matters. In patients taking digoxin, calcium must be given with extreme caution (slow infusion over 20-30 minutes) because calcium enhances the toxicity of digoxin glycoside — the combination can trigger ventricular arrhythmias. For hypocalcemia presenting with tetany, carpopedal spasm, or laryngospasm, 1-2g calcium gluconate IV over 10-20 minutes relieves symptoms rapidly, followed by a maintenance infusion if needed.
